title: Oncall decision lattice for multi-model fallbacks
author: Evelyn Chen
content:
# Purpose

This page documents a decision-lattice (a prescriptive decision tree expressed as a set of prioritized checks) for oncall operators to resolve service-impacting incidents that involve multi-model failures, degradation, or capacity constraints. It is intended for SREs, runtime engineers, and first-responders supporting LLM inference and routing logic.

The lattice helps responders choose safe, deterministic fallback actions that preserve availability and customer SLAs while minimizing cost and regression risk. Use this during a live incident and include the chosen path in the incident timeline for later postmortem analysis.

---

# Summary (TL;DR)

- If primary model is degraded/unavailable, follow the decision-lattice in order.
- Prefer model variants that preserve semantic fidelity (quantized or shorter context variants) before downgrading model family.
- If capacity is root-cause, shift routing by region or capacity tier and enable conservative batching/cache policies.
- Always: communicate to customers using the status templates below, annotate the incident timeline with chosen fallback path, and trigger a postmortem for any SLO breach.

---

# Decision-lattice (stepwise checks)

1) Confirm scope and impact (0-5m)
   - Check alert and dashboard: p99 latency, 5xx rate, error budget burn, per-tenant error spikes.
   - Identify model(s) involved (model-id, model-version, quantization profile).
   - Ownership: oncall -> primary service owner (team) and model steward.

2) Quick containment (5-10m)
   - If error-rate spike is > 0.5% of requests or sustained p99 > 2x SLO for > 5m, enable circuit-breaker for downstream callers and route new traffic to degraded mode.
   - Toggle: /api/feature/enable-degraded-mode (see runbook step below).

3) Evaluate model-level fallbacks (10-20m) — follow in order until the issue is resolved:
   A) Variant swap: switch to the same model architecture with a compatible quantization profile or shorter max_length (keeps behavior consistent).
      - Example: rdm-7b-v2-fp16 -> rdm-7b-v2-8bit; check compatibility table in Runtime Configs.
      - Risk: medium. Expected impact: slight latency improvement, minimal quality regression.

   B) Replica replacement: route to a warmed replica or hot standby in another region / Dedicated pool.
      - Use when localized capacity or noisy neighbors suspected.
      - Command: router.set_route("model-id", pool="dedicated-nyc-1")

   C) Model downgrade: route to a compatible smaller model (same family) with known quality profile.
      - Example path: rdm-34b -> rdm-13b -> rdm-7b.
      - Always attach an evaluation tag to responses to collect quality telemetry.

   D) Graceful degradation: enable cached-prefix responses or static guidance message if no compatible model is available.
      - Example message to client (degraded mode): "We are experiencing higher latency; responses may be abbreviated."

4) Platform-level fallbacks (20-40m)
   - If model-level actions fail, broaden to platform mitigations: autoscale Dedicated pools, enable auxiliary routing to Hosted API (if customer allows), or shift traffic to read-only evaluation endpoints.
   - Check legal/compliance flags before moving customer traffic across deployment boundaries (see Compliance Gate below).

5) Restore & revert (after stabilization)
   - Once p99 latency and error-rate have returned below SLO for 30m, plan a controlled revert following the rollout policy: canary (10%), 30m observation, 50%, 100%.
   - Document exact commands, timestamps, and operators in the incident timeline.

---

# Runbook snippets (commands, checks, and quick play)

- Health checks and triage CLI:

  ```bash
  # cluster health
  ri cluster status --region=us-east-1 --pool=hosted
  # recent error-rate for model
  ri metrics query --metric=error_rate --model=rdm-7b-v2 --window=10m
  # change route
  ri router set --model=rdm-7b-v2 --backend=dedicated-nyc-1
  ```

- Enable degraded mode (feature flag):

  ```bash
  ri flags set degraded-mode=true --scope=organization
  # attach note for audit
  ri flags annotate degraded-mode --note="Enabled by oncall for incident INC-####"
  ```

- Quick fallback example (variant swap):

  1. Verify target variant is compatible: `ri models info rdm-7b-v2-8bit`
  2. Route 100% of new traffic to variant: `ri router set --model=rdm-7b-v2 --variant=rdm-7b-v2-8bit`
  3. Monitor quality telemetry: `ri telemetry tail --tag=variant-swap`

---

# SLOs and thresholds to trigger lattice branches

| SLO / Metric | Threshold | Recommended immediate action |
|---|---:|---|
| p99 inference latency (512 tokens) | > 350ms sustained for 5m | Begin containment; evaluate variant swap and scaling |
| 5xx rate (service) | > 0.5% of requests per 10m | Enable circuit-breakers; route to degraded-mode |
| Error budget burn | > 50% in 24h window | Notify SRE lead; escalate to war room |
| Model-quality telemetry (ROUGE/embedding drift) | Regression vs baseline > 8% | Do not automatically downgrade model-family; open triage with model steward |

Note: SLO thresholds are service-level defaults. Teams owning customer-critical flows may define stricter SLOs in their runbooks.

---

# Compliance Gate (legal/customer constraints)

Before routing customer traffic to a different deployment (e.g., hosted -> dedicated -> partner region) confirm:
- Customer contract allows cross-region routing or regional fallbacks.
- If the customer is under Private deployment, you must obtain oncall-priv-approve from the Private Ops oncall.
- For regulated customers, inform Customer Success before moving traffic; use the customer comm templates below.

Responsible: Oncall -> Private Ops -> Customer Success (escalation if required).

---

# Runbook for Postmortem and Evidence Collection

1) Create the postmortem: template `postmortem/create --incident INC-####` (owner: responder).
2) Attach evidence: graphs (p99 / error-rate), routing changes, command logs, feature flag annotations, sample inputs/outputs for affected tenants.
3) Required fields: impact summary, timeline (with fallback decisions and operators), root cause hypothesis, corrective actions, owners, ETA for fixes.
4) If incident caused customer SLA credit, follow Finance/Legal process: `finance/claims/incident-credit` and attach legal-approved wording.

---

# Game-day scenarios and drill script (recommended cadence)

- Quarterly game-day: simulate "primary model cold restart + noisy neighbor in region X". Objectives:
  - Exercise: variant swap, replica replacement, and customer communication within 20m.
  - Score: time-to-stable (target < 25m), number of manual escalations (target 0-1).

- Drill script (30m):
  1. Inject traffic spike to hosted pool (ops team).
  2. Simulate model replica crash.
  3. Oncall must follow lattice and pick fallback path; observer records deviations.
  4. Debrief and update lattice thresholds if needed.

---

# Status page and customer communication templates

Use these templates on the public/private status pages and in direct customer notifications. Always include: what happened, who is impacted, what we are doing, ETA (if known), mitigation steps, and how customers can reach support.

1) Initial acknowledgement (first 10m):

Subject: [Redwood] Incident impacting inference latency for model {model-id}

Message:
Hello — we are investigating an issue affecting inference latency for {model-id}. Some requests may see increased latency or errors. Our oncall team is actively investigating and implementing fallback routing. We will provide an update within 15 minutes.

2) Ongoing update (every 30m until resolved):

Subject: [Redwood] Update — Incident {INC-####} (impact & mitigation)

Message:
Status: Investigating / Mitigating / Stabilized (choose)
Impact: {brief summary of affected customers/regions}
What we did: {e.g., variant swap to rdm-7b-v2-8bit; enabled degraded-mode}
Next update: in 30 minutes or earlier

3) Resolution & follow-up (post-resolution):

Subject: [Redwood] Resolved — Incident {INC-####}

Message:
Status: Resolved
Summary: The issue was caused by {root cause}. We restored normal routing at {timestamp} and observed SLO conformant behavior for 30 minutes.
Actions taken: {list of fallbacks and restores}
Customer impact: {e.g., brief periods of higher latency; no data loss}
Postmortem link: {link}
If you require further assistance, contact support@redwood.ai

---

# Ownership & escalation matrix (quick)

- First responder: Oncall SRE (engineering) — primary triage, initial containment.
- Model steward: Research/Applied ML — quality triage and rollback guidance.
- Runtime owner: Eng - serving runtime — kernel/kernel selection and perf tuning.
- Private Ops: Eng - private deployments — compliance & cross-deployment routing approval.
- Customer Success: GTM — customer notifications and contract checks.

Escalation rules:
- If impact is > 25% of customers or major enterprise tenant is affected, escalate to Engineering Pager and Schedule an Exec Brief.
- If error budget > 80% burn in 24h, escalate to SRE Director.

---

# Post-incident actions and continuous improvement

- Within 48h: capture lessons learned and assign corrective actions with owners and due-dates.
- Within 7 days: update lattice thresholds or add an automated canary if the incident revealed a blindspot.
- Within 30 days: deliver a regression test to the eval-harness and schedule a follow-up game day.

---
